L01| THE JACKDAW
L02| 
L03| 163
L04| 
L05| The upper parts of the male Jackdaw are glossy black with purple and green
L06| reﬂections; the ear-coverts, nape and sides of neck ashy-grey inclining to white;
L07| under parts dull black; bill and feet black, iris greyish-white. The female is
L08| slightly smaller than the male and has a slightly smaller and duller grey patch
L09| on the nape; her bill is also a triﬂe shorter. The young are dull black, the
L10| grey patch very feebly indicated.
L11| 
L12| There are few places where the Jackdaw cannot ﬁnd a home: coming from
L13| the Continent to England, this bird may be seen in numbers ﬂying in and out of
L14| holes in the cliﬀs of Dover, its incessant cries chack, chack, being a welcome sound;
L15| so also in country or town, in ruined castle or modern palace the Jackdaw is
L16| everywhere to be seen. I must confess that I like the Jackdaw: he is a bird
L17| with considerable sense of humour, and (in spite of much persecution) he seems
L18| to bear no malice. The late Lord Lilford, however, could ﬁnd nothing good to
L19| say of him: the following being some of his remarks respecting the Jackdaw in
L20| his “Birds of Northamptonshire”:—“This amusing but most pernicious bird is
L21| extremely common in our county, and probably only too well-known to most of
L22| our readers. In the hollow trees about the park and pleasure-grounds of Lilford
L23| they used to swarm at the breeding-season, till we found it absolutely necessary
L24| to wage war upon them in the interests of our garden, poultry, and game, to say
L25| nothing of those of the Barn Owl, a species for which we have always entertained
L26| a sincere respect and aﬀection. The Daws not only carried oﬀ numbers of young
L27| chickens, pheasants, and partridges, and committed havoc among our green-peas
L28| and other vegetables, but in several instances, to our knowledge, took possession
L29| of the Owls’ nests, destroyed their eggs, and piled up their own nests in the cavities
L30| selected by the harmless and most useful bird of night; occasionally, however, the
L31| tables are turned, as we have previously mentioned when treating of the Barn Owl.
L32| For these misdemeanours we have for some years past made a practice of shooting
L33| the old Jackdaws and destroying their nests and eggs wherever we found them,
L34| with the result of decided beneﬁt to ourselves and our neighbours. The Jackdaw
L35| disputes the palm for noisy and obtrusive impudence with the House-Sparrow, and
L36| does not, to our knowledge, compensate us in any way for his misdoings. That
L37| the Daw fulﬁls his duties in the great scheme of nature I do not deny, but must
L38| confess that I am unable to discover what they may be.”
L39| 
L40| Seebohm, however, although he admits that it levies blackmail on the Gulls,
L41| says of the Jackdaw:—“It is quite as harmless a bird as the Rook, and at certain
L42| seasons of the year it is very useful. You have but to watch its actions in the
L43| ﬁelds to be convinced of this.”
L44|

Exclude text that only helps to navigate the page: running heads repeated at the top of pages (such as the genus name or chapter title beside a page number), bare plate labels ("PLATE XLV."), page numbers and signatures.

taxon: a scientific (Latin) name of an organism.
- Include binomials and trinomials ("Accentor modularis"), names of a single word at any rank used as the name of a taxon ("Bulimus", "Turdidae"), and an abbreviated genus followed by an epithet ("A. modularis"). Names in capitals or small capitals count ("BULIMUS CASTUS").
- Include the Latin plural of a genus name used for the members of the genus ("these small Bulimi" gives "Bulimi"), and a genus name given in brackets inside a citation ("PFEIFFER, (Glandina,) Pro. Zool. Soc." gives "Glandina").
- The authority after a name is not part of the taxon: for "Accentor modularis (Linn.)" the taxon is "Accentor modularis" and "Linn." is a separate person mention.
- Exclude a bare abbreviated genus that only opens a Latin description ("Bul. testa ...").

vernacular: a common-language name that identifies a particular kind of organism (a species or a named group).

locality: a named real geographic place, in whatever role it appears.
- Include habitat, distribution, collection and observation statements and any other mention of a place. In "Hab. Central America?" the mention is "Central America".

- Exclude publication dates and years in citations ("Pro. Zool. Soc., 1846", "published in April 1890"), general behaviour that is not one event ("arrives in April", "breeds in spring", "most numerous in October and November"), ages, durations and page numbers.

person: any named person, in whatever role: collector or observer, cited author, naming authority (abbreviated or not).

- Label a name by its role at that spot: "ADAMS, MS." gives the person "ADAMS", while "(Mus. Adams.)" is an institution and no person.
- Exclude a person's name that is part of a taxon name ("Cumingii") or of an institution name ("Cuming" in "Mus. Cuming").

- Report the whole name as printed, abbreviations included: "Mus. Cuming", "Mus. Dennison", "British Museum".

L03| THE HOODED CROW
L04| 
L05| birds, nor indeed, in some cases, old ones either, being safe from its prying eyes
L06| and carnivorous propensities. There are, however, one or two instances on record
L07| of its having remained to nest in this neighbourhood, but not of late years.”
L08| 
L09| Mr. Stevenson also quotes the following from St. John’s “Natural History
L10| and Sport in Moray,” p. 59:—“It kills newly-born lambs, picking out the eyes
L11| and tongue while the poor creature is still alive. It preys on young grouse,
L12| partridges, hares, etc., and is very destructive to eggs of all sorts. In certain
L13| feeding spots in the woods I have seen the remains of eggs of the most extra‐
L14| ordinary variety and number. No sooner does a wild duck, pheasant, or any bird
L15| leave its nest, than the Hooded Crow is on the look-out, and I have no doubt
L16| that a single pair often destroys many hundred eggs in the course of a season.
L17| All birds seem aware of this, and Peewits, Gulls, Redshanks, etc., attack most
L18| furiously any Crow which they see hunting near their nests. The ‘hoody’ is
L19| also very fond of young ducks, and destroys great numbers. In the mountains
L20| it is bold enough to make prize of the eggs of the eagle, peregrine falcon, or
L21| osprey, if the parent birds happen to be driven oﬀ their nests.”
L22| 
L23| In their “Notes from Redcar” (“Zoologist,” 1893, p. 6), speaking of the immi‐
L24| gration of Hoodies from the 12th to the 30th of October, Messrs. T. H. Nelson,
L25| and F. Pilling observe:—“The Hoodies are generally noticed in largest numbers
L26| during thick weather in October and November.” According to Seebohm this
L27| species migrates by day, and Gätke says:—“In the autumn, and with favourable
L28| weather, the migration commences at about eight o’clock in the morning, with
L29| ﬂocks of from ﬁfty to one hundred individuals; the movement soon passes into a
L30| stream of ﬂocks, consisting of from a hundred to at least ﬁve hundred examples,
L31| and continues in this manner, without gaps of any kind, until two o’clock in the
L32| afternoon. We can scarcely, in a case of this kind, assume that we are dealing
L33| with a stream or route of migration which just chances to cross Heligoland, for
L34| the movement proceeds in equal magnitude from east to west as far as the eye
L35| can reach. More than this, on days when powerful migrations of this kind take
L36| place, the migration-front or column has been seen from boats eight miles north
L37| of the island to stretch farther to the north, as far as the limits of vision extend;
L38| while on the south it reached, simultaneously and in equal magnitude, up the
L39| Weser, at least as far as Bremerhaven, as was determined from the steamer which
L40| regularly plies between this island and the latter place. We thus get a migration
L41| column of at least thirty-six geographical miles in breadth.”
L42|

L44| which it would be well worth our readers’ while to peruse, but for which we
L45| cannot ﬁnd space here; nevertheless, his concluding paragraphs are, we consider,

L01| THE SKY-LARK
L02| 
L03| 183
L04| 
L05| Practically the Alaudidæ constitute an Old World family, one species only
L06| occurring in North America, whilst, as Jerdon observes, “They are very sparingly
L07| represented in Malayana and Australia.”
L08| 
L09| Family—ALAUDIDÆ.
L10| 
L11| THE SKY-LARK.
L12| 
L13| Alauda arvensis, LINN.
L14| 
L15| FOUND during the summer months throughout the whole of Europe; nesting
L16| in Scandinavia as far north as lat. 70°, whilst in North Africa it breeds
L17| sparingly as far south as the slopes of the Atlas Mountains, and in the
L18| east, in Russia and Siberia, and at high elevations in Japan, the valley of the
L19| Amoor, South-east Mongolia, Turkestan and Persia. In winter it visits China,
L20| North-west India, Afghanistan, Persia, Asia Minor, Palestine and Egypt. It has
L21| been met with at Madeira, and is reputed to have occurred on Greenland. It has
L22| also been introduced into the United States,* New Zealand and Australia.
L23| 
L24| Throughout Great Britain and Ireland, the Sky-Lark is widely distributed,
L25| abundant, and (excepting in the extreme north) resident.
L26| 
L27| The climatic variations of the Sky-Lark have been separated under several
L28| distinctive names, such as A. dulcivox, A. japonica, A. cantarella, A. liopus, A. blak-
L29| istoni, A. gulgula, A. australis, A. cœlivox, A. wattersi, and A. sala; but so many
L30| intergrades exist that Ornithologists generally are now content to regard them as
L31| one variable species.
L32| 
L33| Our Sky-Lark in breeding-plumage has the upper parts golden brown, with
L34| blackish centres to the feathers; edges of greater wing-coverts paler; the outer-
L35| most tail-feather white, with the exception of a blackish streak on the inner web;
L36| 
L37| * One example was also shot in the Bermudas, in 1850.
</page>
